sections.title: A guide you should not follow

blocks.title: How do you recognise a lion? Wait until it roars at you as you die!
blocks.body: This poem pretends to be a helpful guide for identifying wild animals. But every 'test' works only when it is **too late**. **Carolyn Wells** uses this trick to make us laugh.

blocks.title: The poet
blocks.body: **Carolyn Wells** was an American writer of humorous verse, nonsense poems and mystery novels. Her playful poems are full of puns, odd spellings and twists.
blocks.future: Comic writing, advertising and cartooning use the same tricks: surprise, exaggeration and wordplay.

blocks.question: Why is the advice in this poem useless in real life?
options: You can identify each animal only after it has attacked you
The poem gives too many facts
blocks.explanation: That is the joke of the poem.

blocks.title: What the poem says
blocks.body:
The poet tells us how to recognise six wild animals, each in its own stanza, and every time the 'clue' comes too late:

| Animal | How to 'tell' it, according to the poem |
|---|---|
| **Asian Lion** | a large, tawny beast in the jungles of the East; it roars at you as you are dying |
| **Bengal Tiger** | a noble wild beast with black stripes on a yellow ground; notice if he eats you |
| **Leopard** | a beast whose hide is peppered with spots; you know it as soon as it has leapt on you |
| **Bear** | a creature that hugs you very, very hard; if in doubt, it gives one more 'caress' |
| **Hyena and Crocodile** | hyenas come with merry smiles; if they weep, they are crocodiles |
| **Chameleon** | small, like a lizard, no ears or wings; if you see nothing on the tree, it is the chameleon |

**The joke:** each identification comes only when the animal is attacking you. The tone is light and comic; the poem is meant to entertain, not to teach zoology.

blocks.question: How can you identify the Bengal Tiger, according to the poem?
options: by noticing whether it eats you
blocks.explanation: It has black stripes on a yellow ground.

blocks.question: How can you tell a hyena from a crocodile?
options: hyenas come with merry smiles; crocodiles weep

blocks.title: How the poet makes us laugh
blocks.body:
| Device | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Humour / irony** | 'Just notice if he eats you' | the test comes too late |
| **Poetic licence** | 'dyin'' (dying), 'lept' / 'lep' (leapt, leap) | changes spelling to keep rhyme and rhythm |
| **Rhyme scheme** | ababcc in each stanza | a neat, sing-song rhythm |
| **Alliteration** | 'who **h**ugs you very, very **h**ard'; '**B**e sure it is a **B**ear' | music and fun |
| **Pun** | 'caress' for a deadly hug | a gentle word for a dangerous act |
| **Inversion** | 'if there should to you advance a large and tawny beast' | an old-fashioned order that sounds grand |
| **Idiom** | crocodile tears | false tears; the hyena smiles, the crocodile weeps |

blocks.question: Why does the poet write 'dyin'' instead of 'dying'?
blocks.explanation: Poets may bend rules for rhyme and rhythm.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Six animals in order: Lion, Tiger, Leopard, Bear, Hyena/Crocodile, Chameleon.**
- **Every clue comes too late: roar, eat, leap, hug, weep, invisible.**
- **Rhyme: ababcc; poetic licence: dyin', lept, lep.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Taking the poem as serious advice: it is **humorous**.
2. Saying the tiger has spots: the **leopard** has spots; the tiger has black stripes on yellow.
3. Calling 'dyin'' a mistake: it is **poetic licence**.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Students add a new stanza in the same style for another animal (for example, a snake or an elephant), with a clue that comes too late.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Which line in the poem made you laugh the most? Why?

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **The Tale of Custard the Dragon:** another comic poem.
- **A Tiger in the Zoo:** a serious poem about a tiger.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
How does Carolyn Wells use humour in 'How to Tell Wild Animals'? Answer in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** The poem pretends to be a guide to recognising wild animals, but each clue comes too late to help. You will know the Asian Lion when it roars at you as you are dying, and the Bengal Tiger if it eats you. The leopard is known once it has leapt on you, and the bear by its deadly hug, gently called a 'caress'. Hyenas smile while crocodiles weep their famous tears, and the chameleon is recognised when you see nothing at all. The poet also bends spellings ('dyin'', 'lep') to keep the rhyme and rhythm, which adds to the fun. Through irony, wordplay and a light tone, the poem entertains us rather than teaching zoology.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.body:
- The poem 'teaches' how to identify six wild animals.
- Each clue is useful only when the animal attacks, which is the joke.
- Humour comes from irony, puns, poetic licence and a sing-song rhyme.

blocks.title: Exam tips
blocks.body:
- In answers, name the animal and its 'clue'.
- Explain poetic licence with 'dyin'' and 'lep'.
- State clearly that the tone is humorous.

blocks.front: How do you identify a leopard, according to the poem?
blocks.back: By its spotted hide, as soon as it has leapt on you.
A poet's freedom to bend spelling or grammar, as in 'dyin'' and 'lep', for rhyme and rhythm.
